title: Your First Trek in India: A Beginner's Guide From People Who Have Done 1,000+ Camps
excerpt: Never trekked before? Good. Here is how to pick your first trek, get your legs ready and pack without overpacking, from a club that has taken 1,00,000+ people outdoors.
coverAlt: A line of first-time trekkers walking up a green hillside in Himachal

seo.title: First Trek in India: A Beginner's Guide | CNA Camp Blog
seo.description: Never trekked before? How to pick your first trek in India, prepare in 4 weeks, pack in layers and avoid common mistakes. Tips from 1,000+ camps.

faqs.question: What is the best first trek for a beginner in India?
faqs.answer: Pick a short trek at a comfortable height with a fixed campsite. A day trek near home, then a camp with short walks (like our Manali camps), is the easiest way in.

faqs.question: How fit do I need to be for my first trek?
faqs.answer: If you can walk 5 to 6 km at an easy pace, you are ready for most beginner treks. Four weeks of walking and stair climbing is enough preparation.

faqs.question: Can a girl join a trek alone?
faqs.answer: Yes. Solo travellers 18+ can join open batches, and we run girls-only batches with female volunteers.

faqs.question: What should I carry on my first trek?
faqs.answer: Layers (quick-dry T-shirt, fleece, windproof jacket), broken-in trekking shoes, socks, cap, sunglasses, sunscreen, a torch, a water bottle and personal medicines.

markdown:
The most common message we get on WhatsApp is not about price or dates. It is this: "I have never trekked. Will I manage?"

Short answer: yes. Most of the people who have walked with us over the last 20+ years started exactly where you are. Some came with friends who pushed them. Some came alone. Many were sure they would be the slowest in the group, and a few were. Every one of them made it to the top of something.

Here is what we tell them before their first trek.

## 1. Start with the right trip, not the toughest one

Your first trek should leave you tired and happy, not tired and scared. Choose something short, at a comfortable height, with a fixed campsite.

A good order for most beginners:

- **A day trek close to home.** In Gujarat, Osam Hill near Patanvav or a forest walk at Hingolgadh is perfect. You learn how your body feels after 4 to 5 hours on your feet.
- **A camp with short treks.** A few days at one base, with day walks around it. Our Manali camps work this way: you sleep in the same tent every night and come back for lunch.
- **Then a multi-day trek.** Once you know you enjoy it, try a route where you walk to a new campsite most days.

Not sure what the difference is between a trek, a camp and a nature trail? A trek means walking to the view, with a new campsite most days. A camp means one base and activities around it. A nature trail means travelling together with short, easy walks.

@@image campus-02 | Blue tents on a green meadow at a base camp in Himachal

## 2. Get your legs ready (four weeks is enough)

You do not need a gym. You need stairs and a little discipline.

- **Weeks 1 and 2:** walk 30 to 40 minutes, five days a week. Take the stairs everywhere.
- **Weeks 3 and 4:** walk 45 to 60 minutes with a light backpack (3 to 4 kg). Add two sessions of stair climbing, 15 minutes each.
- **Every day:** 10 minutes of stretching for calves, thighs and back.

If you can walk 5 to 6 km at an easy pace without stopping, you are ready for most beginner treks. If you have a medical condition, talk to your doctor before you book, and tell your trek leader too.

## 3. Pack light, pack in layers

The most common beginner mistake is one heavy jacket. Mountain weather changes by the hour, so layers work better.

- **Base layer:** a quick-dry T-shirt (avoid cotton on long walks; it stays wet).
- **Middle layer:** a fleece or a light woollen sweater.
- **Outer layer:** a windproof jacket. For snow trips, a proper down jacket.
- **Feet:** trekking shoes with a good grip, broken in before the trip. Two or three pairs of socks.
- **Small things that matter:** cap, sunglasses, sunscreen, lip balm, a torch, a water bottle and your personal medicines.

Leave the jeans, the third pair of shoes and the hair dryer at home. Nobody on a trail has ever said "I wish I had packed more".

@@image snow-02 | Campers walking up a snowy mountain road in warm layers

## 4. What a trek day actually looks like

People imagine walking from dawn to dark. It is gentler than that. On a typical CNA day you have breakfast, start walking while it is cool, take short breaks every hour, and reach camp or come back for lunch. Afternoons are for a short walk, an activity or rest. Evenings are for food, stories and a sky you cannot see from the city.

Walk at your own pace. A good trek leader keeps one person at the front and one at the back, so nobody is ever alone or in a hurry.

## 5. Five beginner mistakes we see every season

- **New shoes on the trip.** Wear them for at least two weeks before.
- **Drinking too little water because there is "no washroom nearby".** Dehydration makes everything harder.
- **Rushing the first hour.** Start slow. Your body needs 20 minutes to settle in.
- **Ignoring a small blister.** Stop and fix it early.
- **Leaving trash behind.** Carry it in, carry it out.

## 6. Going alone? That is more common than you think

Many first-timers join solo. You are part of a group from the first day, you share meals and tents, and by the second evening you are trading snacks and stories. If you are 18 or older, you can join any of our open batches on your own.

@@image group-11 | A group of campers cheering together in a deodar forest

## Ready for your first one?

Start small, get your legs ready, pack in layers and walk at your own pace. That is honestly most of it. The rest you learn on the trail, usually from the person walking next to you.

**[Browse beginner-friendly trips](/trips)** or [WhatsApp us](https://wa.me/917046361009?text=First%20trek%2C%20where%20should%20I%20start%3F): “First trek, where should I start?”

title: Gujarat's Hidden Nature Spots You Can Reach in a Weekend
excerpt: A coral reef you can walk on, a forest with lions, a hill from the Mahabharata and a salt desert under the full moon. Eight wild corners of Gujarat, and how to see each in a weekend.
coverAlt: Green hills of Saurashtra after the monsoon rains

seo.title: Gujarat Nature Spots for a Weekend Trip | CNA Camp Blog
seo.description: Walk on a coral reef, see Gir's lions, trek Osam Hill and catch the White Rann's full moon. Eight wild Gujarat spots you can reach in a weekend.

faqs.question: Which nature spots in Gujarat can I visit in one day?
faqs.answer: Narara island for the coral reef walk and Osam Hill for a short trek are both day trips from Rajkot. Hingolgadh also works as a day trip, though a night there is better.

faqs.question: What is the best time to visit Gujarat's nature spots?
faqs.answer: It depends on the place. Saputara and Hingolgadh are best in the monsoon (July to September). Gir and the White Rann are best in winter (November to February or March). Narara works on low-tide days.

faqs.question: Can you really walk on a coral reef in Gujarat?
faqs.answer: Yes. At Narara, in the Marine National Park near Jamnagar, the reef is left under knee-deep water at low tide. You walk on a marked route with a guide and never touch or pick anything alive.

faqs.question: Is Gir safe to visit with family?
faqs.answer: Yes. You see the forest from a permitted safari jeep with a forest guide, on fixed routes. Children and older family members can join the safari easily.

markdown:
Gujarat has a coral reef you can walk on. It has the only wild lions in Asia, a sanctuary where about 230 kinds of birds have been seen, and a salt desert so white that the full moon seems to sit on it.

Most of us from Ahmedabad, Rajkot or Surat have seen none of them. We have seen the highway that goes past them, on the way to somewhere "better".

We have taken groups to these places for 20+ years. Here are eight we keep going back to, with the honest catch for each.

A quick note: "weekend" here means one to three days. In Gujarat the season matters more than the distance, so check the months first.

## 1. Narara: a coral reef with no boat and no scuba

Narara is part of the Marine National Park in the Gulf of Kutch, near Jamnagar. When the tide pulls back, the reef is left under knee-deep water and you walk on it with a guide. Look down and you find starfish, crabs, sea anemones and, if you are patient, an octopus changing colour to hide from you.

Our founder's old brochure counted 37 kinds of hard and soft coral here and more than 100 kinds of seaweed. You need closed shoes that can get wet and a low-tide date.

- **Good for:** a day trip, families, school groups
- **The catch:** the tide table picks the date, not you
- **Our trip:** [Narara Island Coral Walk](/trips/narara)

@@image trip:narara | Visitors walking on the coral reef at Narara island during low tide

## 2. Hingolgadh: birds, chinkara and a palace on the hill

Hingolgadh is a small sanctuary in Jasdan taluka of Rajkot district, on hills about 1,000 feet high. It is a birder's place first. About 230 species have been recorded here, and on a slow morning walk you can tick off a surprising number of them. Chinkara live here, along with nilgai, porcupine and mongoose.

On the hilltop stands Hingolgadh Palace, with a small museum of the royal family. Our camps add a night trek, a campfire and plenty of time to learn which bird, tree or snake is which. Stay a night if you can. The forest sounds different after dark.

- **Good for:** first camps, school groups, bird watchers
- **Best time:** right after the monsoon, when the hills turn green
- **Our trip:** [Hingolgadh Nature Camp](/trips/hingolgadh-nature-camp)

## 3. Osam Hill: where the Pandavas hid, two hours from Rajkot

Near Upleta, above the village of Patanvav, Osam Hill carries one of Saurashtra's best stories. Local legend says the Pandavas sheltered here during their exile. People will show you Bhim's giant eating plate and the Bhim Kund, a pool of water on the hill, along with old temples and the remains of a fort.

The real draw for many is the rock. Osam's natural boulders and faces are good for a first try at rock climbing and rappelling. As a trek it is short, green and easy, which makes it one of the best first treks in Gujarat.

- **Good for:** a Sunday trek, first-timers, college groups
- **Best time:** July to February
- **Our trip:** Osam Hill, [Patanvav](/trips/osam-hill)

## 4. Sasan Gir: the last wild home of the Asiatic lion

Gir is the only place on earth where Asiatic lions still live in the wild. The forest also holds around 38 kinds of mammals and about 300 kinds of birds, by our brochure's count.

Our camp runs for two nights. You go on a jeep safari at Devalia, walk along the Hiran river where lions come down to drink, and end the evening around a campfire with the Siddi community's dance. Honest catch: nobody can promise you a lion. The forest decides.

- **Good for:** wildlife lovers, families, friends' groups
- **Best time:** November to March
- **Our trips:** [Sasan Gir Wildlife Camp](/trips/sasan-gir) or [Gir Wildlife and Diu Beach](/trips/gir-diu)

@@image trip:sasan-gir | An Asiatic lion resting in the dry forest of Gir

## 5. Bet Dwarka: an island camp on the Gulf of Kutch

You take a boat from Okha jetty, and the mainland noise drops away. Bet Dwarka is known as the island home of Lord Krishna, and the sea around it is full of life. We stay at a partner campsite on the island, walk through the mangroves, and take a boat out to nearby islands to watch marine life. Lunch on a rocking boat is part of the deal.

- **Good for:** a marine camp with school or college groups
- **Best time:** October to March
- **Our trip:** Marine Camp, [Bet Dwarka](/trips/bet-dwarka-marine-camp)

## 6. Saputara: Gujarat's monsoon hill

If you think Gujarat is flat and dry, go to Saputara in August. It sits at 873 metres in the Sahyadri hills of Dang district, wrapped in forest. In the rains the whole region turns green, and Gira waterfall is at its loudest. Add a forest walk in Vansda National Park.

The catch is distance. From Saurashtra it is a long trip by bus or train via Valsad, so treat it as a long weekend, not a quick one.

- **Good for:** monsoon lovers, families, friends
- **Best time:** July to September
- **Our trip:** Saputara, [Dang Forest](/trips/saputara)

## 7. Kutch and the White Rann

An old Kutchi saying goes something like this: Sorath is best in winter, the rest of Gujarat in summer, but Kutch is good all twelve months. We love the line. We still go to the White Rann in winter, because the salt flat at Dhordo is often under water in the monsoon.

Come on a full-moon night if you can. The salt glows, and you will understand why people drive all the way here. Kalo Dungar, the highest point in Kutch, gives you the view from above.

- **Good for:** friends' groups, photographers, families
- **Best time:** November to February
- **Our trips:** [White Rann of Kutch](/trips/white-rann-of-kutch), [Kutch Nature Camp](/trips/kutch) and [Rann of Kutch and Dholavira](/trips/rann-of-kutch-dholavira)

@@image trip:white-rann-of-kutch | The White Rann salt flat near Dhordo in Kutch at sunset

## 8. Diu: forts, caves and quiet beaches

Diu is a small Union Territory joined to Gujarat by a bridge. Its old name was Dev Patan, and the Portuguese left behind a sea fort, white churches and a town plan worth walking. We walk it all: the caves, the fort walls, Nagoa beach and the sea shrine of Gangeshwar Mahadev.

- **Good for:** an easy coastal break with friends or family
- **Best time:** August to March
- **Our trip:** [Diu Coastal Camp](/trips/diu)

## Which one first?

- **Only have a Sunday?** Narara or Osam Hill.
- **First camp for a child or a school group?** Hingolgadh.
- **Want wildlife?** Gir, between November and March.
- **Monsoon weekend?** Saputara or Hingolgadh.
- **Winter full moon?** The White Rann.

## A few rules for every wild place

Carry your plastic back home. Do not feed animals or pick up coral and shells. Keep your voice down in the forest and your speaker at home. These spots stayed "hidden" partly because people were kind to them. Let us keep it that way.

## Plan your Gujarat weekend

Pick the season first, then the place. Closed shoes, a cap and a water bottle go to all of them. Every trip page has its own carry list for the rest.

**[See all Gujarat trips](/destinations#gujarat)** or [WhatsApp us](https://wa.me/917046361009?text=Which%20Gujarat%20trip%20suits%20this%20month%3F): “Which Gujarat trip suits this month?”

title: Himalayan Trek Packing List: What to Carry (and What to Leave)
excerpt: A practical, layer-by-layer packing list for Himalayan treks and camps, what changes between a summer trip and a snow trip, and the packing mistakes we see every season.
coverAlt: Sunrise lighting up snow peaks above the Manali valley

seo.title: Himalayan Trek Packing List: What to Carry | CNA Camp Blog
seo.description: A layer-by-layer Himalayan trek packing list for summer and snow treks, what to leave at home and the mistakes to avoid. From 20+ years on the trail.

faqs.question: What should I pack for a Himalayan trek?
faqs.answer: Three layers (quick-dry T-shirts, a fleece, a windproof jacket), trek pants, broken-in trekking shoes, 4 to 5 pairs of socks, caps, gloves, sunglasses, sunscreen, a torch, a water bottle, your medicines and your original photo ID.

faqs.question: What extra do I need for a snow trek?
faqs.answer: Two sets of thermal inner wear, a down jacket, waterproof shoes and gloves, extra woollen socks and dark sunglasses for snow glare.

faqs.question: Can I wear jeans on a trek?
faqs.answer: Better not. Jeans are heavy, stiff when wet and slow to dry. Trek pants or track pants are lighter and much more comfortable.

faqs.question: How heavy should my trek bag be?
faqs.answer: As light as you can manage. If you can carry it comfortably up a few floors of stairs, you are close. Most people pack a third more than they need.

markdown:
Try this tonight. Lay out everything you plan to take on your Himalayan trek, on the bed, in one place. Now put a third of it back in the cupboard.

That is roughly the gap between what first-timers pack and what they actually use. After 20+ years of walking groups through Himachal, Sikkim and Nepal, we can tell you that the person with the smallest bag is usually the happiest one on day three. A heavy bag does not keep you warm. The right three layers do.

Here is the list we would give a friend.

## The idea behind the list: layers, not bulk

Mountain weather can swing from hot sun to cold wind inside an hour, so you dress in layers and add or remove them as you go.

- **Base layer:** what touches your skin. Quick-dry T-shirts by day, thermal inner wear for cold nights and snow trips.
- **Mid layer:** what traps warmth. A fleece jacket or a light woollen sweater.
- **Outer layer:** what blocks wind and rain. A windproof, water-resistant jacket. On snow trips, add a down jacket.

Three thin layers keep you warmer than one thick jacket, and they dry faster too.

## The core list for any Himalayan trek

### Clothing

- 3 to 4 quick-dry T-shirts (one for each two days of walking is plenty)
- 2 trek pants (not jeans) and one comfortable pair for camp
- 1 fleece or woollen sweater
- 1 windproof or rain jacket
- 1 set of thermal inner wear (2 sets for snow)
- A night dress you do not walk in, so you always have something dry to sleep in

### Feet

- Trekking shoes with good grip, already broken in
- 4 to 5 pairs of socks, at least two of them woollen
- Floaters or sandals for camp and for wet days

### Head and hands

- A cap for the sun and a woollen cap for the cold
- Gloves (woollen for summer nights, waterproof for snow)
- Sunglasses with UV protection

### Health and care

- Your personal medicines, with a copy of the prescription
- Sunscreen and lip balm (the mountain sun burns faster than you think)
- A small kit: plasters, blister pads, ORS sachets
- Toothbrush, small soap, a quick-dry towel

### Small things that matter

- A torch or headlamp, with spare batteries
- A 1-litre water bottle (two for high treks)
- A small daypack for the walk, with a rain cover
- A few plastic or zip bags for wet clothes and trash
- Your original photo ID card. Hotels, permits and checkpoints ask for the original.

@@image trek-02 | A line of campers trekking up a green Himalayan hillside

## Summer trek vs snow trek: what changes

The core list stays the same. These are the additions.

### Summer (April to June, and October)

Days are warm, nights are cool, and you may get rain. Trips like our Astro Adventure Trekking Camp in Manali mix treks with river crossing and rafting, so you will get wet on purpose.

- Extra quick-dry clothes, since something will always be drying
- Mosquito repellent for the lower valleys
- Strong sunscreen and a cap with a brim
- Light bedding (a bed sheet and an air pillow) for train and bus nights

### Snow (December to March)

On our Manali Snow Camp, you spend the day on skis, a snowboard or a snow trail. Cold is the main job of your bag.

- 2 sets of thermal inner wear
- A down jacket on top of your fleece
- Waterproof shoes, plus woollen socks to change into every evening
- Waterproof gloves and a spare pair of woollen gloves
- Dark sunglasses: snow reflects the sun, and snow glare hurts your eyes

@@image campus-03 | CNA's Manali campus buildings with snow peaks behind

## Going higher: Sikkim and Everest Base Camp

The higher you go, the less room there is for mistakes in your bag.

- **Sikkim:** the Sikkim Trek drives up to Tsomgo lake at about 3,750 metres, and the eastern Himalaya gets more rain than Himachal. A proper rain jacket and a rain cover for your bag are not optional here.
- **Everest Base Camp:** Base Camp sits at 5,364 metres, and the dawn walk to Kala Patthar starts in the dark and the cold. Add a down jacket, a sleeping bag liner, a good headlamp and two water bottles. Indian trekkers need a passport or a voter ID card for Nepal, so carry the original.

At height, drink more water than you feel like drinking, walk slowly, and tell your trek leader early if you get a headache or feel sick. Do not hide it to keep up with the group.

## What to leave at home

- **Jeans.** Heavy when dry, heavier when wet, and slow to dry.
- **Cotton everything.** Cotton holds sweat and gets cold.
- **A third pair of shoes.** Trekking shoes and floaters cover it.
- **Big bottles of shampoo and lotion.** Take small ones or share.
- **Jewellery and costly gadgets.** They only give you something to worry about.
- **A trolley bag.** Wheels do not work on mountain paths. A backpack or a duffel does.
- **Big food stocks.** You will be fed. A few dry fruits or chikki for the walk are enough.

## Packing mistakes we see every season

- **Gloves and cap at the bottom of the bag.** The cold hits at the first stop, and you unpack everything on the roadside to find them.
- **No rain cover.** One shower and every layer in the bag is wet.
- **Only a photo of your ID on the phone.** Many checkpoints want the original.
- **Medicines packed in the big bag that goes on the bus roof.** Keep them in your daypack.
- **Skipping sunscreen because it is cold.** Snow and height burn you faster, not slower.
- **New socks never worn before.** They slip and give blisters. Wear them at home first.

## How to pack the bag itself

Heavy things go in the middle, close to your back. Things you need on the walk (jacket, water, snacks, sunscreen, medicines) go in the daypack. Pack each type in its own bag inside the backpack, so you can find your socks at 6 am without emptying everything in a dark tent.

@@image river-02 | A group of campers crossing a mountain river together on a summer trek

## Your trip has its own list

This is a general list. Every trip page on our site has its own "What to carry" section, and your trek leader confirms it before you leave. When in doubt, pack light and pack in layers. You will not miss what you left behind.

**[See Himalayan treks and camps](/destinations#across-india)** or [WhatsApp us](https://wa.me/917046361009?text=Can%20you%20check%20my%20packing%20list%3F): “Can you check my packing list?”

title: Is a School Camp Safe? 8 Things Parents Should Check
excerpt: Before you sign the consent form, ask these eight questions. A practical checklist for parents and teachers, for any school camp with any organiser.
coverAlt: Camp leaders talking to a group of young campers before an activity

seo.title: Is a School Camp Safe? 8 Checks for Parents | CNA Camp Blog
seo.description: Before you sign the camp consent form, check these 8 things: leaders, medical plan, insurance, supervision, gear, stay, briefing and Plan B for weather.

faqs.question: How do I know if a school camp is safe?
faqs.answer: Check eight things: trained leaders, a medical plan with a doctor and ambulance access, insurance, adult supervision with female staff for girls, certified gear, clean stay and food, a briefing before the camp, and a clear plan for bad weather.

faqs.question: Is it safe to send a girl on a school camp?
faqs.answer: Yes, when the organiser sends female volunteers to stay with girls' groups and gives separate stay and toilets. Ask about both before you sign.

faqs.question: Do school camps include insurance?
faqs.answer: Not always. Ask directly. At CNA, camps longer than 5 days include mediclaim cover for the camp period.

faqs.question: What age is right for a first school camp?
faqs.answer: It depends on the child and the trip. Start with a short camp close to home, like a one-night nature camp, before a long trip to the mountains.

markdown:
The consent form from school asks for one signature. Before you give it, ask eight questions.

We say this as people who run school camps. Over 20+ years and 1,000+ camps, we have met two kinds of parents: the ones who sign straight away, and the ones who call us with a list. We like the second kind. Their children are usually the best prepared too.

This checklist works for any organiser, including us. A good one will be glad you asked. A vague answer is an answer too.

## 1. Who leads the camp, and what have they done before?

Ask who will be with the children on the ground, not who runs the office. How many years have they led groups? Are the instructors for climbing, rappelling or river crossing trained for that activity?

At CNA, every activity is led by trained instructors, and our leaders have years of camps behind them. Whoever you go with, ask for names, not adjectives.

## 2. What happens if a child gets hurt or falls ill?

This is the question that matters most, and the answer should be specific. Look for three things:

- A proper medical kit at the camp, not just a few plasters
- A doctor nearby, and the name of the nearest hospital
- A way to get there fast: ambulance access, or a vehicle on standby

At our camps, there is a medical kit at every camp, a doctor nearby and ambulance access for emergencies. Also ask how and when you will be told if your child is unwell.

## 3. Is there insurance for the camp?

Many short camps have no insurance at all. Ask plainly. For our camps longer than 5 days, we arrange mediclaim cover for the camp period. For shorter camps, check what your family's own health policy covers outside your city.

@@image climb-03 | A camper rappelling down a rock face on a rope with safety gear

## 4. Who looks after girls, and who looks after boys?

Ask how many adults travel per group of children, and who they are. Then ask the question many parents feel shy about: who stays with the girls at night?

The right answer is clear. In our camps, female volunteers stay with girls' groups, male volunteers with boys' groups, and both with mixed groups. Schools also send their own teachers, which adds a familiar face.

## 5. Is the adventure gear certified and checked?

Ropes, harnesses, helmets and life jackets are not places to save money. Ask whether the gear is certified, how old it is, and who checks it before each session. We use ISI-marked safety equipment. Any organiser should be able to tell you what standard their gear meets.

## 6. Where will they sleep, eat and wash?

Children cope with simple stays. They do not cope well with bad water or no toilets. Ask:

- Is the stay a tent, a dorm or a hotel? Is the site owned, a partner site or hired?
- Are the toilets attached or nearby, and are they separate for girls and boys?
- Is drinking water safe, and is the food cooked fresh on site?
- Is the bedding washed for each group?

Our Manali campus, for example, has Swiss tents and rooms with attached toilets, drinking water and our own kitchen. Every organiser should be able to describe the site this clearly, with photos.

@@image food-02 | Cooks preparing fresh food in a camp kitchen

## 7. Will there be a briefing before the camp?

A good camp starts before the bus leaves. There should be a meeting with the group (and ideally the parents) that covers the plan, the rules, the packing list, the emergency contacts and any medical needs.

We hold a group meeting before every camp, where the rules are set. Use it. Tell the leader about allergies, asthma, fears or a recent illness. Something you mention in two minutes can save a lot of worry later.

## 8. What happens when the plan changes?

In the mountains and on the coast, plans change. Rain closes a road, a river runs high, the tide comes in early. Ask the organiser: who decides to change the day, and how will parents hear about it?

The right instinct is to change the plan, not push through it. Weather, roads or a tired group can change the day on our camps too, and that is how it should be. Be wary of anyone who promises that everything on the itinerary will happen no matter what.

## A few things to check yourself

Some of the checks are yours, not the organiser's.

- The organiser is a registered body, and you know who backs it. (CNA is backed by Saurashtra Education & Charitable Trust.)
- Your child's medical form is honest and complete.
- Your child knows the leader's name and the one rule that matters most: never go off alone.
- You have the leader's number, not just the school office number.
- Your child has packed for the actual weather, not for a photo.

## Also talk to your child

Ask what excites them and what worries them. A child who is scared of the dark, the water or heights is not a child who should stay home. They are a child the leader should know about. Most fears shrink fast in a group of friends, with a trained adult close by.

@@image group-01 | A group of girls on a school trip in the hills of Himachal

## The short version

A safe school camp has trained leaders, a real medical plan, the right adults with the right children, checked gear, a clean stay, a proper briefing and the good sense to change plans. Ask about all eight. Then let your child go and come back with stories.

**[Planning a school camp? See how we run them](/group-trips#schools)** or [WhatsApp us](https://wa.me/917046361009?text=We%20are%20a%20school.%20Can%20we%20talk%20about%20safety%3F): “We are a school. Can we talk about safety?”
